Trivially, we can do character-based tokenization i.e. mapping each character to a unique number. For example, \mathsf {chr}(97) = \text {``a''} and \mathsf {ord}(\text {``a''}) = 97. The compression ratio will be > 1 because each token corresponds to a character potentially consisting of more than one byte.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. There is a fundamental tradeoff between compression ratio and vocabulary size. As an example, suppose we map every sequence of n bytes to a token. This would achieve a compression ratio of n. However, this would require 256^n tokens in our vocabulary.
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Problem 2 was not entirely straight-forward to me. This actually reminds me of an idea from my information theory course, where we can assume we are given a "prior" over human language then we want to map low-probability characters to large strings in order to minimize the expected length (see huffman coding).

In byte-based tokenization, each byte is a token achieving a compression ratio of exactly 1, where a byte \mapsto [0, 256] . This is very elegant in the sense that our vocabulary size is fixed at 256.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Problem. However, with this, the length of our encoding is the number of bytes in the string, which will become too long.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In word-based tokenization, we simply split the string into the corresponding words then map each of these to a unique integer.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Problem. The vocabulary size is "unbounded" i.e. if we see a word we have not seen before then we need to extend the vocabulary size.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: For the byte pair encoding (BPE), we instead train the tokenizer on raw text to automatically determine the vocabulary.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. In GPT2, they first split the raw text into words and then do this byte pair encoding.

Remark. There are a few additional implementation details to consider for project 1.
\mathsf {encode} loops over all merges. Only loop over merges that matter.
Detect and preserve special tokens (e.g. <|endoftext|>)
Use pre-tokenization (GPT2 regex)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We start by discussing a few essential questions one hopes to answer when they set out to train a large model.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Question. How long to train a 70b parameter model on 15T tokens on 1024 H100s?

html:div.html:details: Answer.Mysteriously, we spawn from the ether (will be explained later) that total_flops = 6 * 70e9 * 15e12. Intuitively, we know that we need to perform some computation for each parameter for each token. However, the 6 is still an ominous mystery. Given the total flops, we then can just take the GPUs FLOP/s multiply by the number of seconds in the day and divide total_flops by this number i.e. days = total_flops / flops_per_day

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. In practice, we must also consider the model flop utilization (MFU). Basically, our algorithm cannot utilize the entirety of the maximum FLOP/s provided by the hardware due to things like memory bandwidth, etc. To account for this in the calculation, they just take flops_per_day / 2.
Question. What is the largest model that you can train on 8 H100s using AdamW?

html:div.html:details: Answer. An H100 has 80gb of shared memory i.e. h100_bytes = 80e9. The calculation then proceeds as # parameters, gradients, optimizer state bytest_per_param = 4 + 4 + (4 + 4) num_parameters = (h100_bytes * 8) / bytes_per_parameter what we need each of parameters, gradients, optimizer state will become clear later.

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. In practice, we also need to account for activations, which will depend on both batch size and sequence length.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Tensor Memory. Tensors are stored as a floating point number. Memory is determined by (i) number of values in tensor and (ii) data type of each value.

float16: here, we decrease both the fraction and exponent bits. Importantly, there are only 5 exponent bits making the effective range (2^{-6}, 2^{6}). The dynamic range for small numbers is pretty bad. This can cause small numbers to "die" effectively killing these neurons for the remainder of learning due to backpropagation.
bfloat16: to fix the problems with float16, they instead keep 8 exponent bits and reduce the fraction bits to 7. This maintains the same dynamic range as float32 while still only using 16 bits.

fp8: Two variants
E4M3: has 4 exponent bits and 3 mantissa bits
E5M2: has 5 exponent bits and 2 mantissa bits Requires modern Hopper Architecture i.e. H100 to perform operations. Also supported by TPUs.

html:ol.html:li: float32 training works but requires lots of memory
Using lower precision data types allows you to train larger models due to lower memory requirements, but can cause instability
To optimize this tradeoff, use mixed-precision training.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In pytorch, tensors are contiguous blocks of memory, where their shape is controlled by strides. A stride basically just refers to how far you have to jump in physical memory to correspond to incrementing the logical index i.e. in a (2, 3) matrix each row requires jumping 3 spots in physical memory. Thus, stride[1] = 3.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. Calling .view((m, n)) just changes the stride but does not modify the physical memory. If you call .view that results in a non-contiguous view, then you cannot call .view again because it assumes contiguous indexing to properly adjust the strides. To deal with this, they have .contiguous() and .reshape() is basically .contiguous().view().
Remark. All elementwise operations make a copy i.e. x + y. A useful function for masked attention is triu().

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
Einops is a useful python library to keep track of high-dimensional matrix operations i.e. matmuls over batch_size, seqlen, etc. High level overview
Initialize like X[float.tensor, "batch seq hidden"] = torch.tensor((2, 3, 4))
Can perform matmul with named dims like z = einsum(x, y, "batch seq1 hidden, batch seq2 hidden -> batch seq1 seq2")
reduce: x = reduce(x, "x y z -> x y 1") is just like mean(x, axis=-1)
rearrange: x = rearrange(x, "... (heads hidden1) -> ... heads hidden 1")

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We refer to the total number of floating point operatings as FLOPS. Alternatively, we refer to the number of floating point operations per second as FLOP/s.
Given a promised FLOP/s, the model flop utilization is given by \frac {\text {actual FLOP/s}}{\text {promised FLOP/s}}

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Example. Performing a matrix multiplication A \cdot B for A \in \mathbb {R}^{(B \times D)} and B \in \mathbb {R}^{(D \times K)}, requires 2 \times B \times D \times K FLOPS

fr:mainmatter.html:p: I hope to do a formal blog touring optimizers because I have written a paper on deep learning optimizers for my optimization course. Due to this, I will leave this blank for now. A brief list of the covered concepts are below:
A key formula to remember: \text {total memory} \approx 4 \times (\text {params} + \text {activations} + \text {grad size} + \text {optimizer state size})

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. Another useful trick is to use low precision for forward pass activations, then use float32 for gradients and network parameters.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Pre-norm vs. Post-norm. The first architecture variation discussed is when to apply the layer norm. As can be seen in the figure below, rather than apply the layer norm in the residual stream. They instead place it before the FFN and MHA layers.
They actually found that adding layer normalization before and after the MHA and FFN works the best. This is known as double norm.
RMSNorm vs. LayerNorm. Another useful trick is to use the RMSNorm instead of LayerNorm.

The RMS norm is simply the layer norm without the added bias term and centering i.e. \mathrm {RMSNorm}: \mathbb {R}^d \to \mathbb {R}^d, \quad \mathbf {x} \mapsto \frac {\mathbf {x}}{\sqrt {\mathrm {Var}[\mathbf {x}_i] + \epsilon }}*\gamma . This is used to spare memory movement of layernorm, where the bias term \beta \in \mathbb {R}^d and has been found to be empirically almost if not as good.
One might wonder if matrix multiplies are the only thing that matters what can such a small change really accomplish.

html:ul.html:li: Due to memory movement, despite being .17% of FLOPS, provided 25% speedup in runtime!!

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. Most people apparently just drop the bias term and keep the centering i.e. subtracting the mean. This makes sense because computing the mean does not require loading any additional information back to memory.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Despite a long list of activations, the two focused on are ReLU and GELU.

The rectified linear unit(ReLU) is defined as \mathrm {ReLU} : \mathbb {R}^d \to \mathbb {R}^d, \quad \mathbf {x} \mapsto \max (0, \mathbf {x}), where the \max is done elementwise i.e. \mathrm {ReLU}(\mathbf {x})_i = \max (0, x_i) This provides "nice" gradients, making it common when training neural networks.

The Gaussian Error Linear Unit (GELU) is a slight modification to the ReLU to account for the non-differentiability at 0. Namely, \mathrm {GELU}(\mathbf {x}) : \mathbb {R}^d \to \mathbb {R}^d, \quad \mathbf {x} \mapsto \mathbf {x} \cdot \psi (\mathbf {x}), where \psi (\mathbf {x}) = \mathrm {CDF}(\mathcal {N}(\mathbf {x}, \mathbf {I}))

html:figure.html:figcaption: GELU vs. ReLU activation and derivative. Taken from here.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The Swish activation is given by \mathrm {Swish}(\mathbf {x}) : \mathbb {R}^d \to \mathbb {R}^d, \quad \mathbf {x} \mapsto \mathbf {x} s(\mathbf {x}), where s : \mathbb {R}^d \to \mathbb {R}^d is the sigmoid function.

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. The extra computation required by GELU or Swish is a non-factor because FLOPS are dominated by matrix multiplication and there is no increase in memory pressure.

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
A gated linear unit is an activation function combined with an elementwise multiplication i.e.
\mathrm {ReGLU} = \mathrm {ReLU}(\mathbf {x}) \otimes \mathbf {V} \mathbf {x},
\mathrm {SwiGLU} = \mathrm {Swish}(\mathbf {x}) \otimes \mathbf {V} \mathbf {x}, where \mathrm {ReLU} is the ReLU activation and \mathrm {Swish} is the Swish activation respectively.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. The matrix \mathbf {V} introduces additional learnable parameters. Therefore, an architecture that uses gating typically reduces their other parameters by a factor of \frac {2}{3}.

fr:title.text: Gating splits the up-projection in two

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Gating splits the up-projection in two

fr:mainmatter.html:p: For one Transformer layer with a gated MLP, what are the parameter count and training FLOPs — and why is the coefficient three rather than two?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Parameters: 3DF, from W_{in1}[D,F], W_{in2}[D,F], W_{out}[F,D].
Training FLOPs: 18BTDF — three matmuls at 6BTDF each, by the 6NPM rule.
Where the third matrix comes from. A Gated Linear Unit (GLU) splits the up-projection into two matrices whose outputs are multiplied elementwise, \sigma (AW_{in1}) \odot (AW_{in2}), so one of them acts as a gate on the other. LLaMA, DeepSeek and most current models do this. A non-gated MLP has a single W_{in} and so 2DF params — and typically scales D and F up to compensate, which is why the two families cost about the same at equal quality.
The gate itself is O(BTF) — elementwise, no contraction, and negligible against BTDF.

fr:title.text: Computing FFN and MHA in parallel is free speedup

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Computing FFN and MHA in parallel is free speedup

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Another small trick is to parallelize computation. Traditionally, one computes the \mathrm {MHA} output and then passes this to the \mathrm {FFN} i.e. \mathbf {y} = \mathbf {x} + \mathrm {FFN}(\mathrm {LN}(\mathbf {x} + \mathrm {MHA}(\mathrm {LN}(\mathbf {x})))). However, this requires waiting for the \mathrm {MHA} to complete before performing the \mathrm {FFN} computation. It has been found that performing these in parallel does not cause any severe degradation in performance. Explicitly, instead they do \mathbf {y} = \mathbf {x} + \mathrm {FFN}(\mathrm {LN}(\mathbf {x})) + \mathrm {MHA}(\mathrm {LN}(\mathbf {x}))

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: What is the role of weight decay in training large models?

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Since there is so much data, it is not feasible to train your model for multiple epochs. This is actually nice in the sense that we do not have to worry about overfitting and performing regularization.

However, many of the large models are still trained with weight decay. Tatsu claims that this is not to do with regularization but actually due to some weird interaction with the learning rate schedule. I am not sure I entirely understood this part.

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Notation. For this section, our notion of an embedding is a function f that takes a token and a position i.e. f(x, i) is the embedding of token x, occurring at position i.

Insight. The inner product of two embeddings should only need relative positioning i.e. for any two \mathbf {x}, \mathbf {y} with positions i and j respectively, there should exist some g, such that \langle f(\mathbf {x}, i), f(\mathbf {y}, j) \rangle = g(\mathbf {x}, \mathbf {y}, i - j) Namely, this can be written as a function of just the relative positioning between the embeddings.
fr:mainmatter.html:p: The simplest transformation that only preserves this relative information are rotations.

html:figure.html:figcaption: Rotating embeddings does not change relative position.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: However, rotations are only easily defined for \mathbb {R}^2. To get around this, they simply partition their input 2d slices and apply the rotation via \mathrm {ROT} = \begin {bmatrix} \cos m \theta _{1} & - \sin m \theta _{1} & & & \\ \sin m \theta _{1} & \cos m \theta _{1} & & & \\ & & \cos m \theta _{2} & -\sin m \theta _{2} & \\ & & \sin m \theta _{2} & \cos m \theta _{2} & \\ & & & & \ddots \end {bmatrix}
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. The \theta _i's are fixed and chosen according to some schedule to capture different "frequencies".
fr:mainmatter.html:p: The embedding are used by appling them to the query and key matrices separately i.e. W_K = \mathrm {ROT}(W_K), \quad W_Q = \mathrm {ROT}(W_Q) These are then what is used in self-attention.
A lot of deep learning is empirical magic. A quick look behind the curtain into this magic awaits below...

The softmax is ill-behaved due to the exponentials. In the transformer, we have two softmaxes: one at the end and one in the attention.
For the first, note \log \sigma (\mathbf {x})_i = \log (x_i) - \log \underbrace {\sum _{j=1}^{d} e^{x_j}}_{D(\mathbf {x})} The only problem is the denominator term. The idea is to enforce the D(\mathbf {x}) = 1 by regularizing via a penalty on \log D(\mathbf {x}) ie. \mathcal {L}_{\text {aux}} = 10^{-4} \log ^2(D(\mathbf {x})) With the \nabla D(\mathbf {x}) should be 0 and we are effectively only considering the non-exponential term.
For the attention, they primarily operate on the logits prior to the softmax. One way is via layer norm before the softmax. Another is via Softcapping

fr:title.text: POTW: Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: POTW: Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Notes on the paper Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need.

For,
b batch dimension,
n sequence length,
d hidden dimension,
h number of heads. The total FLOPS for attention are roughly bnd^2. This comes from
3nd^2 FLOPS to compute Q = XW_Q, K = XW_K, V = XW_V.
Need to do this b times for each input in batch. and the total memory accesses are roughly \underbrace {bnd}_{X} + \underbrace {bhn^2}_{\text {softmax}} + \underbrace {d^2}_{\text {projection}}. This gives high arithmetic intensity O\left (\left (\frac {h}{d} + \frac {1}{bn}\right )^{-1}\right )

However, if we do incremental inference then we must multiply our total number of memory accesses by n i.e. bn^2d + nd^2. This gives arithmetic intensity O\left (\left (\frac {n}{d} + \frac {1}{b}\right )^{-1}\right ), which requires large batch and short sequence length.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. I believe we just ignore the softmax memory contribution in the inference case because it does not scale with n anymore as we are computing the logits just for the next token. Therefore, it becomes a \frac {d}{h} term, which we can safely ignore?
fr:mainmatter.html:p: The key is that the \frac {n}{d} term comes from the bn^2d term, where we are loading h (b \times n \times d / h) K and V matrices n times. Thus, we can improve the \frac {n}{d} term by a factor of h by simply not using a different K and V matrix for each head. This is the entire idea behind MQA.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. Similar to the KV-cache, we still can use h Q matrices because we do not need to load n of them into memory because only the last one matters for inference.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Group query attention is the same idea as MQA but instead of using one K and V for every head, they use a group of them. Where obviously the number of groups needs to be less than the number of heads.

html:figure.html:figcaption: Grouped query uses subset of K and V matrices.

fr:title.text: GQA saves cache, not projection FLOPs

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: GQA saves cache, not projection FLOPs

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Per layer, what do the QKVO projections cost in parameters and training FLOPs under Group Query Attention with N query heads, K key/value heads, and head dimension H?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Parameters: 2D(N+K)H, from W_Q[D,N,H] and W_O[N,H,D] at DNH each, plus W_K, W_V[D,K,H] at DKH each.
Training FLOPs: 12BTD(N+K)H — each projection is 6BTD \cdot (\text {heads}) \cdot H.
The variants are one knob. K = N is plain multi-head attention; K = 1 is MQA; 1 < K < N with K \mid N is grouped-query, with group size G = N/K.
Read the formula for what shrinking K actually buys. It touches only the K term, so the projection cost falls from 2N to N + K — at most a factor of two, and usually far less. That is not why anyone uses GQA. The payoff is the KV-cache, which scales with K alone and is the binding constraint at generation time.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Also inspired by this idea of reducing the dependence of K and V on the sequence length is sliding window attention.

The idea behind sliding window attention is to ensure the number of weight matrices needed for the keys K and values V does not scale with the sequence length. Intuitively, this means allowing each word to "attend" to only some fixed number of previous words rather than the whole sequence

html:figure.html:figcaption: "the" only sees "on" and "sat" rather than the full sentence.

fr:title.text: Scaling Book: Exercises › Sharded Matrices and How to Multiply Them

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Scaling Book: Exercises › Sharded Matrices and How to Multiply Them

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
Consider an array fp32[1024, 4096] with sharding A[I_{XY},J] and mesh {'X': 8, 'Y': 2}. How much data is held by each device? How much time would it take to load this array from HBM on H100s (assuming 3.4e12 memory bandwidth per chip)?
Solution
The notation indicates that we are sharding the first axis (1024) across both x and y? This means we are dividing into fp32[64, 4096] chunks or 4\cdot 64\cdot 4096 bytes per device, which would then take \frac {4\cdot 64\cdot 4096}{3.4e12} = .308 \mu s

Let A be an array with shape int8[128, 2048], sharding A[I_{XY},J], and mesh Mesh({'X': 2, 'Y': 8, 'Z': 2}) (so 32 devices total). How much memory does A use per device? How much total memory does A use across all devices?
Solution
Since there is no sharding across the Z axis. I assume this means it is replicated. This still gives 8\cdot 2048 bytes per device but now total memory is still multiplied by 32 giving 32\cdot 8\cdot 2048 bytes across all devices.

How long does it take to perform the AllGatherY([EY, F]) → [E, F] on a TPU v5e with a 2D mesh {'X': 8, 'Y': 4}, for E = 2048, F = 8192 in bf16? What about for E = F = 256?
Solution
For the large E and F, we will clearly not be latency bound, so we can just perform the ICI cost. We will have N = 2\cdot 2048\cdot 8192 bytes and the TPU v5e uni-directional bandwidth is 4.5e 10. Since we are only gathering over 1 dimension, we do not get any additional bandwidth. Thus, it will take \frac {N}{4.5e10} = 3.72\text {ms}.
For the small E and F, we now need to consider the latency time given by T_{\text {latency}} = \frac {|Y|\cdot T_{\min }}{2} = 2\mu s.
Computing the ICI cost, we have N = 2\cdot 256\cdot 256 bytes and T_{\text {ICI}} = \frac {N}{4.5e 10} = 0.73 \mu s. Thus, the total time is T = \max \{T_{\text {latency}}, T_{\text {ICI}} = 2\mu s.
Remark. I divided the latency time by 2, when once again the TPU v5e sub-mesh does not support wrap-around links and therefore the hop count is NOT upperbounded by |Y|. Also the hop count is actually |Y| - 1 not |Y|, so the correct answer was just T_{\text {min}}\cdot (|Y| - 1) = 3\mu s.

An array is sharded A[I_X,J,K,…] (i.e., only sharded across X ), with a mesh Mesh({'X': 4, 'Y': 8, 'Z': 2}). What is the ratio of the total number of bytes taken up by A across all chips to the size of one copy of the array?
Solution It is sharded across X, so that on each chip there is only 1/4 of A. However, it must be replicated across Y and Z which are 8\cdot 2 = 16 copies. This leaves us with 16 \times the total number of bytes across all copies.

How long should \text {AllGather}_{X}([B_X,D_Y]) take on a TPU v4p 4x4x4 slice with mesh Mesh({'X': 4, 'Y': 4, 'Z': 4}) if B=1024 and D=4096 in bfloat16? How about \text {AllGather}_{XY}([B_X,D_Y]) How about \text {AllReduce}_{Z}([B_X,D_Y]\{U_Z\})?
Solution
We cannot use bi-directional because we are on a non-16 dim axes on TPU v4p. Therefore, the ICI bandwidth is W_{\text {ICI}} = 4.5e10. From AllGather, we know that the communication time is independent of |X| and is \frac {N}{W_{\text {ICI}}}. For this problem, we have N = 1024\cdot 4096\cdot 2. Thus, it will take .186\text {ms}.
Remark. I do not understand wrap-around rules at allor maybe they are just highly unintuitive, but we actually do have bi-directional bandwidth. I also needed to take into consideration that |X| cancels out but we only have N/|Y| bytes. Correct answer is \frac {1024\cdot 4096\cdot 2}{9e10\cdot |Y|}
In this case, we now have double the bandwidth because we are reducing across both dimensions. However, the total number of bytes is now 4\times , which means this will be double the previous part.
An AllReduce requires each device to send the full A across Z. This should be \frac {2BD}{W_{\text {ICI}}} or 2 \times the previous part.
Remark. Completely misunderstood this question. For starters, when reducing along the Z axis, we still stay sharded across x and y and therefore do not make hops across those links. Therefore, we must divide by |X| \cdot |Y|. Also, I guess the heuristic that AllReduce is roughly 2 \times AllGather is used in calculations, which gives final answer \frac {4BD}{|X|\cdot |Y|\cdot W_{\text {ICI}}}

Let’s say we’re performing an \text {AllGather}_X([B_X]) but B is very small (say 128). How long should this take on a TPU v4p 4x4x4 slice with mesh Mesh({'X': 4, 'Y': 4, 'Z': 4}) in bfloat16?
Solution
Since |X| = 4, the hop latency time is \approx 4 \mu s. We have N = 2\cdot 128 = 256bytes and W_{\text {ICI}} = 9e10. This gives .0028 \mu s. So we are severely latency bound.
Remark. Only need to do 2 hops in bi-directional case, so true answer is \approx 2\mu s: still latency bound.

To perform X[B,D]\cdot _D Y[D_X,F] \to Z[B,F], in this section we tell you to perform \text {AllGather}_X(Y[D_X,F]) and multiply the fully replicated matrices (Case 2, Strategy 1). Instead, you could multiply the local shards like X[B,D_X]\cdot _D Y[D_X,F] \to Z[B,F]\{U_X\} (Case 3, Strategy 2), and then \text {AllReduce}_X(Z[B,F]\{U_X\}). How many FLOPs and comms does each of these perform? Which is better and why?
Solution
Case 2, strategy 1. In this case, the AllGather will take \frac {DF}{W_{\text {ICI}}} for communication over ICI and BD + DF + BF over HBM with 2BDF FLOPs.
Case 3, strategy 2. For local shards, each will only need to do \frac {2BDF}{X} FLOPs and BD + D_X F + BF HBM cost. However, the ICI cost would then be the whole matrix which is X \times as much over ICI.
Remark.
I was roughly correct. However, an important distinction (and gap in my understanding I gues) is that we have been ignoring HBM cost when communicating over ICI because these transfers are done concurrently and are therefore bottlenecked by the slower one (ICI).

Let’s say I want to do a matmul A[I,J]\cdot JB[J,K]\to C[I,K] on a TPU v4p 4x4x4 with the lowest possible latency. Assume the inputs can be sharded arbitrarily but the result should be fully replicated. How should my inputs be sharded? What is the total FLOPs and comms time?
Solution
My initial intuition is we do not want to shard along the contracting dimension. If we have a large enough matrix, then I think the best sharding strategy would be to shard A[I_{XYZ}, J], B[J, K]. The multiplication then requires no communication, and the only communication is an AllGather across all 3 axis, which should triple bandwidth. Since we shard over every axis of our mesh, we do not have any additional replicated bytes. This gives us N = 2IKbytes in bf16. Since we are on a 4\times 4\times 4 cube, we have bi-directional bandwidth availability. Therefore, the communication time on TPU v4p is \frac {2IK}{3\cdot 9e10}. The total flops is still just 2IJK.

A typical Transformer block has two matrices W_{in}[D,F] and W_{out}[F,D] where F \gg DF \gg D . Say we have a batch size B. Then the full block is In[B,D]\cdot W_{in}[D,F]\cdot W_{out}[F,D]. Let’s pick D=8192 , F=32768, and B=128 and assume everything is in bfloat16. Assume we’re running on a TPU v5e 2x2 slice but let’s pretend each TPU only has 300MB of free memory. How should In, W_{in}, W_{out}, and Out be sharded to stay below the memory limit while minimizing overall time? How much time is spent on comms and FLOPs? Hint: the final output doesn’t need to be fully replicated, but it should be sharded the same as the input so the “layer” can be repeated.
Solution
To start, lets compute how big everything is.
\begin {align*} In &= 2\cdot B\cdot D \\ &= 2\cdot 8192\cdot 128 = 2^{21} \\ W_{in} &= 2\cdot D\cdot F \\ &= 2\cdot 8192\cdot 32768 = 2^{29} \\ W_{out} &= 2\cdot D\cdot F \\ &= 2\cdot 8192\cdot 32768 = 2^{29} \end {align*}
and each TPU has 300MB \approx 300 \cdot 2^{20} \approx 2^{28} in this example. Therefore, each TPU can fit just over one half of W_{in} and W_{out}, which leads us to have to fully shard both across X and Y. The remaining 11 \cdot 2^{22} can fit \text {In}. However, we need to satisfy the constraint that \text {Out} is sharded in the same way as \text {In}. We adopt the following strategy:
Shard \text {In}[B_{XY}, D], W_{in}[D,F_{XY}]
First, we need to AllGather \text {In} along B.
Then, we have \text {In}[B, D]\cdot W_{in}[D, F_{XY}]\to \text {Tmp}[B, F_{XY}]
Shard W_{out}[F_{XY}, D]
Now we have \text {Tmp}[B, F_{XY}]\cdot W_{out}[F_{XY}, D] \to \text {Out}[B, D]\{U_{XY}\}
Then we need to do a ReduceScatter over XY in the B axis to get back to our input shape.
Now lets count up the communication cost.
First, we have an AllGather over XY of \text {In}. This is N = 2\cdot B\cdot D bytes. We only have unidirectional bandwidth. However, we are gathering over 2 axes, which doubles our bandwidth. Thus, this will take \frac {2\cdot 128\cdot 8192}{2\cdot 4.5e 10} = 23.3\mu s
Then we have a ReduceScatter of \text {Out}[B, D]\{U_{XY}\}, which takes the same time as AllGather and is another 23.3 \mu s.
Thus, the whole communication cost is only 46.6 \mu s.
Remark. In the solution, they instead propose to shard \text {In}[B, D_{XY}], which is equivalent in communication cost. According to Claude, there is a subtle distinction.
If you are in decoding (i.e. B = 1), then you cannot even shard along B but can still shard along D.
However, it seems preferable to shard over B if you can. This way, for activations / reductions over D you do not need any communication.

Above we claimed that when only one input to a matmul is sharded along its contracting dimension, we should AllGather the sharded matrix and perform the resulting contraction locally. Another strategy you might think of is to perform the sharded matmul and then AllReduce the result (as if both inputs were sharded along the contracting dimension), i.e. A[I,J_X]\cdot _J B[J,K]\to C[I,K] by way of
C[I, K]\{U_{X}\} = A[I, J_{X}]\cdot B[J_{x}, K]
C[I, K]\{U_{X}\} = \text {AllReduce}(C[I,K]\{U_{X}\}) Answer the following
Explicitly write out this algorithm for matrices A[N,M] and B[M,K], using indices to show exactly what computation is done on what device. Assume A is sharded as A[I,J_X] across ND devices, and you want your output to be replicated across all devices.
Now suppose you are ok with the final result not being replicated on each device, but instead sharded (across either the N or K dimension). How would the algorithm above change?
Looking purely at the communication cost of the strategy above (in part 2, not 1), how does this communication cost compare to the communication cost of the algorithm in which we first AllGather A and then do the matmul?
Solution
On the device, we can only make use of the J_{X} rows of B and compute the corresponding partial sums. This corresponds to the outer product C'[i] = \sum _{n=i\cdot \frac {J}{ND}}^{i(\frac {J}{ND} + 1)} A_{:,n} \oplus B_{n,:}
The above algorithm would change by replacing the AllReduce with a ReduceScatter. This is better communication wise because AllReduce is two collectives, not one.
The communication cost is the same because ReduceScatter has the same communication cost as AllGather, but it is likely preferable if you are compute bound because you can distribute computation across devices.
Remark. In the solutions, they make the (excellent) point that in the ReduceScatter case we are sending the output N\times K matrix, whereas in the AllGather case we are sending the N\times M matrix. Therefore, if we have a large contraction dim, then the second case might also be preferable.

In the table above, it was noted that the time to perform an AllToAll is a factor of 4 lower than the time to perform an AllGather or ReduceScatter (in the regime where we are throughput-bound). In this problem we will see where that factor of 4 comes from, and also see how this factor would change if we only had single-direction ICI links, rather than bidirectional ICI links.
Let’s start with the single-direction case first. Imagine we have D devices in a ring topology and want to do either an AllGather or a ReduceScatter on an N x N matrix A[I_X,J] (say D divides N for simplicity). Describe the comms involved in these two collectives, and calculate the total number of scalars (floats or ints) which are transferred across a single ICI link during the entirety of this algorithm.
Now let’s think about an AllToAll, still in the single-directional ICI case. How is the algorithm different in this case than the all-gather case? Calculate the number of scalars that are transferred across a single ICI link in this algorithm.
You should have found that the ratio between your answers to part (a) and part (b) is a nice number. Explain where this factor comes from in simple terms.
Now let’s add bidirectional communication. How does this affect the total time needed in the all-gather case?
How does adding bidirectional communication affect the total time needed in the AllToAll case?
Now simply explain the ratio between AllGather time and AllToAll time in a bidirectional ring.
Solution
The communication involved in either of these collectives is each chip in the ring sending a chunk of A of size \frac {N^2}{D} to the right neighbor. A single ICI link sees every chunk and therefore N^2(D-1) scalars must cross a single ICI link. The D - 1 comes from the fact that each device already owns one \frac {N^2}{D} chunk.
AllToAll differs than AllGather because each subsequent forwarding is \frac {N^2}{D^2} less bytes. Namely, each device has an \frac {N^2}{D} shard of A. Then in AllToAll, you forward to a neighbor who takes a \frac {1}{D} of this chunk and forwards the remaining. Therefore, a single ICI link only sees the following bytes of ICI traffic \frac {N^2}{D} \sum _{i=1}^{D} (D - i) = \frac {N^2\cdot D(D-1)}{2D} = \frac {N^2(D-1)}{2}
From the previous 2 parts, we see that the ratio is exactly \frac {1}{2}. This comes from the fact that, for farther devices, a link needs to transfer a much smaller number of bytes in AllToAll. Whereas, in AllGather, you must see all bytes of a chunk for every device uniformly.
In the AllGather case, bidirectional communication still requires each link to see every byte. Therefore, only the ICI bandiwdth changes and not the total bytes seen per-link.
In the AllToAll case, each chip only needs its sub-chunk of each chunk. Therefore, we can divide the chunk into the front and back half and send in each direction. This halves the total bytes seen per link, reducing to \frac {N^2(D-1)}{4}.
In the bidirectional case, we can effectively reduce our AllToAll to 2 unidirectional AllToAll's of half the size. This then halves the bytes-per-link, which was already half of an AllGather. Since every device needs every byte of each chunk in the AllGather case, it gets no reduction in the bidirectional case.

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
A gated linear unit is an activation function combined with an elementwise multiplication i.e.
\mathrm {ReGLU} = \mathrm {ReLU}(\mathbf {x}) \otimes \mathbf {V} \mathbf {x},
\mathrm {SwiGLU} = \mathrm {Swish}(\mathbf {x}) \otimes \mathbf {V} \mathbf {x}, where \mathrm {ReLU} is the ReLU activation and \mathrm {Swish} is the Swish activation respectively.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. The matrix \mathbf {V} introduces additional learnable parameters. Therefore, an architecture that uses gating typically reduces their other parameters by a factor of \frac {2}{3}.

fr:title.text: Gating splits the up-projection in two

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Gating splits the up-projection in two

fr:mainmatter.html:p: For one Transformer layer with a gated MLP, what are the parameter count and training FLOPs — and why is the coefficient three rather than two?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Parameters: 3DF, from W_{in1}[D,F], W_{in2}[D,F], W_{out}[F,D].
Training FLOPs: 18BTDF — three matmuls at 6BTDF each, by the 6NPM rule.
Where the third matrix comes from. A Gated Linear Unit (GLU) splits the up-projection into two matrices whose outputs are multiplied elementwise, \sigma (AW_{in1}) \odot (AW_{in2}), so one of them acts as a gate on the other. LLaMA, DeepSeek and most current models do this. A non-gated MLP has a single W_{in} and so 2DF params — and typically scales D and F up to compensate, which is why the two families cost about the same at equal quality.
The gate itself is O(BTF) — elementwise, no contraction, and negligible against BTDF.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Given a promised FLOP/s, the model flop utilization is given by \frac {\text {actual FLOP/s}}{\text {promised FLOP/s}}
Formal notebook for my journey in Stanford's CS336 as part of my LLM self-study endeavors.

Trivially, we can do character-based tokenization i.e. mapping each character to a unique number. For example, \mathsf {chr}(97) = \text {``a''} and \mathsf {ord}(\text {``a''}) = 97. The compression ratio will be > 1 because each token corresponds to a character potentially consisting of more than one byte.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. There is a fundamental tradeoff between compression ratio and vocabulary size. As an example, suppose we map every sequence of n bytes to a token. This would achieve a compression ratio of n. However, this would require 256^n tokens in our vocabulary.
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Problem 2 was not entirely straight-forward to me. This actually reminds me of an idea from my information theory course, where we can assume we are given a "prior" over human language then we want to map low-probability characters to large strings in order to minimize the expected length (see huffman coding).

In byte-based tokenization, each byte is a token achieving a compression ratio of exactly 1, where a byte \mapsto [0, 256] . This is very elegant in the sense that our vocabulary size is fixed at 256.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Problem. However, with this, the length of our encoding is the number of bytes in the string, which will become too long.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In word-based tokenization, we simply split the string into the corresponding words then map each of these to a unique integer.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Problem. The vocabulary size is "unbounded" i.e. if we see a word we have not seen before then we need to extend the vocabulary size.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: For the byte pair encoding (BPE), we instead train the tokenizer on raw text to automatically determine the vocabulary.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. In GPT2, they first split the raw text into words and then do this byte pair encoding.

Remark. There are a few additional implementation details to consider for project 1.
\mathsf {encode} loops over all merges. Only loop over merges that matter.
Detect and preserve special tokens (e.g. <|endoftext|>)
Use pre-tokenization (GPT2 regex)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We start by discussing a few essential questions one hopes to answer when they set out to train a large model.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Question. How long to train a 70b parameter model on 15T tokens on 1024 H100s?

html:div.html:details: Answer.Mysteriously, we spawn from the ether (will be explained later) that total_flops = 6 * 70e9 * 15e12. Intuitively, we know that we need to perform some computation for each parameter for each token. However, the 6 is still an ominous mystery. Given the total flops, we then can just take the GPUs FLOP/s multiply by the number of seconds in the day and divide total_flops by this number i.e. days = total_flops / flops_per_day

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. In practice, we must also consider the model flop utilization (MFU). Basically, our algorithm cannot utilize the entirety of the maximum FLOP/s provided by the hardware due to things like memory bandwidth, etc. To account for this in the calculation, they just take flops_per_day / 2.
Question. What is the largest model that you can train on 8 H100s using AdamW?

html:div.html:details: Answer. An H100 has 80gb of shared memory i.e. h100_bytes = 80e9. The calculation then proceeds as # parameters, gradients, optimizer state bytest_per_param = 4 + 4 + (4 + 4) num_parameters = (h100_bytes * 8) / bytes_per_parameter what we need each of parameters, gradients, optimizer state will become clear later.

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. In practice, we also need to account for activations, which will depend on both batch size and sequence length.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Tensor Memory. Tensors are stored as a floating point number. Memory is determined by (i) number of values in tensor and (ii) data type of each value.

float16: here, we decrease both the fraction and exponent bits. Importantly, there are only 5 exponent bits making the effective range (2^{-6}, 2^{6}). The dynamic range for small numbers is pretty bad. This can cause small numbers to "die" effectively killing these neurons for the remainder of learning due to backpropagation.
bfloat16: to fix the problems with float16, they instead keep 8 exponent bits and reduce the fraction bits to 7. This maintains the same dynamic range as float32 while still only using 16 bits.

fp8: Two variants
E4M3: has 4 exponent bits and 3 mantissa bits
E5M2: has 5 exponent bits and 2 mantissa bits Requires modern Hopper Architecture i.e. H100 to perform operations. Also supported by TPUs.

html:ol.html:li: float32 training works but requires lots of memory
Using lower precision data types allows you to train larger models due to lower memory requirements, but can cause instability
To optimize this tradeoff, use mixed-precision training.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In pytorch, tensors are contiguous blocks of memory, where their shape is controlled by strides. A stride basically just refers to how far you have to jump in physical memory to correspond to incrementing the logical index i.e. in a (2, 3) matrix each row requires jumping 3 spots in physical memory. Thus, stride[1] = 3.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. Calling .view((m, n)) just changes the stride but does not modify the physical memory. If you call .view that results in a non-contiguous view, then you cannot call .view again because it assumes contiguous indexing to properly adjust the strides. To deal with this, they have .contiguous() and .reshape() is basically .contiguous().view().
Remark. All elementwise operations make a copy i.e. x + y. A useful function for masked attention is triu().

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
Einops is a useful python library to keep track of high-dimensional matrix operations i.e. matmuls over batch_size, seqlen, etc. High level overview

Can perform matmul with named dims like z = einsum(x, y, "batch seq1 hidden, batch seq2 hidden -> batch seq1 seq2")

rearrange: x = rearrange(x, "... (heads hidden1) -> ... heads hidden 1")

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We refer to the total number of floating point operatings as FLOPS. Alternatively, we refer to the number of floating point operations per second as FLOP/s.
Given a promised FLOP/s, the model flop utilization is given by \frac {\text {actual FLOP/s}}{\text {promised FLOP/s}}

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Example. Performing a matrix multiplication A \cdot B for A \in \mathbb {R}^{(B \times D)} and B \in \mathbb {R}^{(D \times K)}, requires 2 \times B \times D \times K FLOPS

fr:mainmatter.html:p: I hope to do a formal blog touring optimizers because I have written a paper on deep learning optimizers for my optimization course. Due to this, I will leave this blank for now. A brief list of the covered concepts are below:
A key formula to remember: \text {total memory} \approx 4 \times (\text {params} + \text {activations} + \text {grad size} + \text {optimizer state size})

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. Another useful trick is to use low precision for forward pass activations, then use float32 for gradients and network parameters.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Pre-norm vs. Post-norm. The first architecture variation discussed is when to apply the layer norm. As can be seen in the figure below, rather than apply the layer norm in the residual stream. They instead place it before the FFN and MHA layers.
They actually found that adding layer normalization before and after the MHA and FFN works the best. This is known as double norm.
RMSNorm vs. LayerNorm. Another useful trick is to use the RMSNorm instead of LayerNorm.

The RMS norm is simply the layer norm without the added bias term and centering i.e. \mathrm {RMSNorm}: \mathbb {R}^d \to \mathbb {R}^d, \quad \mathbf {x} \mapsto \frac {\mathbf {x}}{\sqrt {\mathrm {Var}[\mathbf {x}_i] + \epsilon }}*\gamma . This is used to spare memory movement of layernorm, where the bias term \beta \in \mathbb {R}^d and has been found to be empirically almost if not as good.
One might wonder if matrix multiplies are the only thing that matters what can such a small change really accomplish.

html:ul.html:li: Due to memory movement, despite being .17% of FLOPS, provided 25% speedup in runtime!!

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. Most people apparently just drop the bias term and keep the centering i.e. subtracting the mean. This makes sense because computing the mean does not require loading any additional information back to memory.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Despite a long list of activations, the two focused on are ReLU and GELU.

The rectified linear unit(ReLU) is defined as \mathrm {ReLU} : \mathbb {R}^d \to \mathbb {R}^d, \quad \mathbf {x} \mapsto \max (0, \mathbf {x}), where the \max is done elementwise i.e. \mathrm {ReLU}(\mathbf {x})_i = \max (0, x_i) This provides "nice" gradients, making it common when training neural networks.

The Gaussian Error Linear Unit (GELU) is a slight modification to the ReLU to account for the non-differentiability at 0. Namely, \mathrm {GELU}(\mathbf {x}) : \mathbb {R}^d \to \mathbb {R}^d, \quad \mathbf {x} \mapsto \mathbf {x} \cdot \psi (\mathbf {x}), where \psi (\mathbf {x}) = \mathrm {CDF}(\mathcal {N}(\mathbf {x}, \mathbf {I}))

html:figure.html:figcaption: GELU vs. ReLU activation and derivative. Taken from here.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The Swish activation is given by \mathrm {Swish}(\mathbf {x}) : \mathbb {R}^d \to \mathbb {R}^d, \quad \mathbf {x} \mapsto \mathbf {x} s(\mathbf {x}), where s : \mathbb {R}^d \to \mathbb {R}^d is the sigmoid function.

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. The extra computation required by GELU or Swish is a non-factor because FLOPS are dominated by matrix multiplication and there is no increase in memory pressure.

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
A gated linear unit is an activation function combined with an elementwise multiplication i.e.
\mathrm {ReGLU} = \mathrm {ReLU}(\mathbf {x}) \otimes \mathbf {V} \mathbf {x},
\mathrm {SwiGLU} = \mathrm {Swish}(\mathbf {x}) \otimes \mathbf {V} \mathbf {x}, where \mathrm {ReLU} is the ReLU activation and \mathrm {Swish} is the Swish activation respectively.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. The matrix \mathbf {V} introduces additional learnable parameters. Therefore, an architecture that uses gating typically reduces their other parameters by a factor of \frac {2}{3}.

fr:title.text: Computing FFN and MHA in parallel is free speedup

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Computing FFN and MHA in parallel is free speedup

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Another small trick is to parallelize computation. Traditionally, one computes the \mathrm {MHA} output and then passes this to the \mathrm {FFN} i.e. \mathbf {y} = \mathbf {x} + \mathrm {FFN}(\mathrm {LN}(\mathbf {x} + \mathrm {MHA}(\mathrm {LN}(\mathbf {x})))). However, this requires waiting for the \mathrm {MHA} to complete before performing the \mathrm {FFN} computation. It has been found that performing these in parallel does not cause any severe degradation in performance. Explicitly, instead they do \mathbf {y} = \mathbf {x} + \mathrm {FFN}(\mathrm {LN}(\mathbf {x})) + \mathrm {MHA}(\mathrm {LN}(\mathbf {x}))

However, many of the large models are still trained with weight decay. Tatsu claims that this is not to do with regularization but actually due to some weird interaction with the learning rate schedule. I am not sure I entirely understood this part.

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Notation. For this section, our notion of an embedding is a function f that takes a token and a position i.e. f(x, i) is the embedding of token x, occurring at position i.

Insight. The inner product of two embeddings should only need relative positioning i.e. for any two \mathbf {x}, \mathbf {y} with positions i and j respectively, there should exist some g, such that \langle f(\mathbf {x}, i), f(\mathbf {y}, j) \rangle = g(\mathbf {x}, \mathbf {y}, i - j) Namely, this can be written as a function of just the relative positioning between the embeddings.
fr:mainmatter.html:p: The simplest transformation that only preserves this relative information are rotations.

html:figure.html:figcaption: Rotating embeddings does not change relative position.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: However, rotations are only easily defined for \mathbb {R}^2. To get around this, they simply partition their input 2d slices and apply the rotation via \mathrm {ROT} = \begin {bmatrix} \cos m \theta _{1} & - \sin m \theta _{1} & & & \\ \sin m \theta _{1} & \cos m \theta _{1} & & & \\ & & \cos m \theta _{2} & -\sin m \theta _{2} & \\ & & \sin m \theta _{2} & \cos m \theta _{2} & \\ & & & & \ddots \end {bmatrix}
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. The \theta _i's are fixed and chosen according to some schedule to capture different "frequencies".
fr:mainmatter.html:p: The embedding are used by appling them to the query and key matrices separately i.e. W_K = \mathrm {ROT}(W_K), \quad W_Q = \mathrm {ROT}(W_Q) These are then what is used in self-attention.
A lot of deep learning is empirical magic. A quick look behind the curtain into this magic awaits below...
Exception 1. in the case of GLUs, we recall that to account for extra parameters we scale \frac {2}{3}. Therefore, d_{\text {ff}} = \frac {8}{3}d_{\text {model}}.
Exception 2. In T5, they use d_{\text {ff}} = 64d_{\text {model}}. The logic for this was that we could maximize the MFU by increasing matrix size. Ended up going back to small d_{\text {model}}.

Rule 3. Aspect ratio = \frac {d_{\text {model}}}{n_{\text {layer}}} \approx 100-200
Pipeline dependent: if network speed is fast than parallelizing is easier and shallow networks are better.
If poor network speed then pipeline parallel might be more viable and deeper networks would be more parallelizable.

Rule 4. Vocab size
For single language models, vocab size is typically 30-50k

The softmax is ill-behaved due to the exponentials. In the transformer, we have two softmaxes: one at the end and one in the attention.
For the first, note \log \sigma (\mathbf {x})_i = \log (x_i) - \log \underbrace {\sum _{j=1}^{d} e^{x_j}}_{D(\mathbf {x})} The only problem is the denominator term. The idea is to enforce the D(\mathbf {x}) = 1 by regularizing via a penalty on \log D(\mathbf {x}) ie. \mathcal {L}_{\text {aux}} = 10^{-4} \log ^2(D(\mathbf {x})) With the \nabla D(\mathbf {x}) should be 0 and we are effectively only considering the non-exponential term.
For the attention, they primarily operate on the logits prior to the softmax. One way is via layer norm before the softmax. Another is via Softcapping

fr:title.text: POTW: Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: POTW: Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Notes on the paper Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need.

For,
b batch dimension,
n sequence length,
d hidden dimension,
h number of heads. The total FLOPS for attention are roughly bnd^2. This comes from
3nd^2 FLOPS to compute Q = XW_Q, K = XW_K, V = XW_V.
Need to do this b times for each input in batch. and the total memory accesses are roughly \underbrace {bnd}_{X} + \underbrace {bhn^2}_{\text {softmax}} + \underbrace {d^2}_{\text {projection}}. This gives high arithmetic intensity O\left (\left (\frac {h}{d} + \frac {1}{bn}\right )^{-1}\right )

However, if we do incremental inference then we must multiply our total number of memory accesses by n i.e. bn^2d + nd^2. This gives arithmetic intensity O\left (\left (\frac {n}{d} + \frac {1}{b}\right )^{-1}\right ), which requires large batch and short sequence length.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. I believe we just ignore the softmax memory contribution in the inference case because it does not scale with n anymore as we are computing the logits just for the next token. Therefore, it becomes a \frac {d}{h} term, which we can safely ignore?
fr:mainmatter.html:p: The key is that the \frac {n}{d} term comes from the bn^2d term, where we are loading h (b \times n \times d / h) K and V matrices n times. Thus, we can improve the \frac {n}{d} term by a factor of h by simply not using a different K and V matrix for each head. This is the entire idea behind MQA.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. Similar to the KV-cache, we still can use h Q matrices because we do not need to load n of them into memory because only the last one matters for inference.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Group query attention is the same idea as MQA but instead of using one K and V for every head, they use a group of them. Where obviously the number of groups needs to be less than the number of heads.

html:figure.html:figcaption: Grouped query uses subset of K and V matrices.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Per layer, what do the QKVO projections cost in parameters and training FLOPs under Group Query Attention with N query heads, K key/value heads, and head dimension H?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Parameters: 2D(N+K)H, from W_Q[D,N,H] and W_O[N,H,D] at DNH each, plus W_K, W_V[D,K,H] at DKH each.
Training FLOPs: 12BTD(N+K)H — each projection is 6BTD \cdot (\text {heads}) \cdot H.
The variants are one knob. K = N is plain multi-head attention; K = 1 is MQA; 1 < K < N with K \mid N is grouped-query, with group size G = N/K.
Read the formula for what shrinking K actually buys. It touches only the K term, so the projection cost falls from 2N to N + K — at most a factor of two, and usually far less. That is not why anyone uses GQA. The payoff is the KV-cache, which scales with K alone and is the binding constraint at generation time.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Also inspired by this idea of reducing the dependence of K and V on the sequence length is sliding window attention.

The idea behind sliding window attention is to ensure the number of weight matrices needed for the keys K and values V does not scale with the sequence length. Intuitively, this means allowing each word to "attend" to only some fixed number of previous words rather than the whole sequence

html:figure.html:figcaption: "the" only sees "on" and "sat" rather than the full sentence.
